physical.physical_description: Watercolour with ink on a prepared red ground, depicting a young man seated, reading a book. The red square sheet has been collaged at a diagonal onto a white backing sheet. The image has sections blocked in white, details in black linework and stippling, and some parts coloured in yellow and green. The man depicted is light-skinned with short black hair, and sits on a chair which has wide armrests, floral finials, and a rattan-woven back. He wears a white, long-sleeved barong with a standing collar and half-placket with three yellow buttons; a pair of green, white and yellow vertical-striped trousers; and a pair of yellow shoes. Underneath the image is a white caption block in the shape of a heart; on this are five lines of verse lettered in black, written in a Filipino language. At the top of the red sheet is a marking which reads, ‘B./ 1’.
physical.summary: This watercolour, made by an unknown artist from the Philippines, is among the earliest objects to enter the V&A’s collection. In lines of rhyming verse, they add a playful tone and more nuanced, often humorous, layer of personality. Some words are transliterated using Spanish spellings, which, along with the mixing of native and European fashions, exposes legacies of Empire in the form and fabric of these objects. The works evidence Manila as a cosmopolitan Southeast Asian capital – and a complex fusion of East and West – in the 1800s, as it is today.

physical.title: Barong
physical.medium_raw: Plain weave piña silk with whitework embroidery, cotton threads, synthetic threads; lined with polyester organza
physical.physical_description: This man's shirt, known as barong tagalog or barong, is made of plain weave piña silk, using piña (pineapple fibre) as the warp threads and silk as the weft wefts. It has a stiffened turn down collar, buttoned up on central front, long sleeves with cuffs, and lined with white polyester organza. Size: L. It is fully embellished with hand embroidery of scrolls and leaf motifs arranged in stripes format extending from the front to the sleeves and across the back panel in the style of the 'Raya' design. 'Raya' is derived from the Spanish word meaning "stripe." Two types of whitework embroidery techniques are used: the "embossed" design (burda) is done in white cotton threads; while the drawn thread work (calado) is done by tying several threads in the weave to create the designs, the thread used to tie the "calado" is synthetic.
physical.summary: This man’s shirt, known as a barong Tagalog or simply barong, is worn untucked over trousers as formal dress in the Philippines. It is made from piña silk, a fine fabric woven from a blend of pineapple fibre and silk, and decorated with whitework embroidery known as calado. This technique involves carefully drawing together individual threads to create delicate openwork patterns. Such embroidery is traditionally handcrafted by highly skilled embroiderers in Lumban, Laguna Province, south of Manila. The barong was popularised as national formal wear by President Ramon Magsaysay (1907–1957), who wore it for his inauguration and other state occasions. This example was worn by the young donor at diplomatic galas with his wife, Stacy Danika Garcia, who serves as Third Secretary and Vice Consul at the Embassy of the Philippines in London, as well as at other formal events, including celebrations marking Philippine National Day.
